entities.summary:
Paweł Włodkowic (c. 1370, Brudzeń Duży – 1435), a towering figure in early 15th-century European intellectual and political life, served as a Polish scholar, jurist, statesman, and rector of the Kraków Academy. His profound contributions to international law, particularly his articulation of a doctrine of religious tolerance and the just war theory, challenged the prevailing crusading ideology of the Teutonic Knights and significantly influenced diplomatic discourse at the Council of Constance. Włodkowic's advocacy for the rights of non-Christian peoples, specifically the pagan Samogitians and Lithuanians, positioned him as a radical voice against forced conversion and territorial expansion disguised as religious zeal.

Włodkowic's most celebrated moment came during the Council of Constance (1414-1418), where he presented his seminal treatise, *Tractatus de potestate papae et imperatoris respectu infidelium* (Treatise on the Power of the Pope and the Emperor Regarding Infidels). In this work, he meticulously argued that pagan nations possessed the right to self-governance and property, and that conversion should only occur through peaceful persuasion, not military conquest. His arguments directly confronted the Teutonic Order's claims to legitimate their invasions of Baltic lands, asserting that even the Pope lacked the authority to authorize wars of aggression against non-Christians who had committed no offense. He also served as an envoy for King Władysław II Jagiełło, skillfully navigating complex ecclesiastical and political landscapes.
